The Shape Of Export Controls To Come

AJ Cortese, Laila Khawaja
16 Nov 2026

For the past four years, Washington policymakers and the US AI industry have been split over a big question. Should the US tightly restrict China’s access to advanced computing capacity, in order to solidify its lead in the AI race? Or should it sell more chips and equipment to China, in order to lock China into dependence on US hardware, and support open-weight AI models? The sudden fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, the biggest commercial champion of diffusion, has shifted power in Washington to the restrictionists. A bipartisan majority now supports more export controls, both to contain China and to rein in what many see as the corruption that has tainted Trump’s tech policies. Today’s China Tech Brief examines what is on the menu.

Gavekal Technologies: Chips

The Nvidia Blast Zone

Laila Khawaja, Arthur Kroeber
12 Nov 2026

The Nvidia scandal looks sure to topple CEO Jensen Huang and put the company on a very rocky course for a few months. The headlines have focused on the romantic and spy stories, but the crucial issues lie elsewhere. The big risk for Huang and Nvidia is that they might be found guilty of breaking US export control rules by colluding in the illegal transshipment of AI chips from Singapore to China. The Chinese AI industry, which already has a tough time getting enough advanced chips, could soon find it even tougher, as there is a good chance that the US Congress will soon act to tighten up export controls.

Permitting Reform’s Big Chance

10 Nov 2026

Efforts to clean up the US’s sclerotic system for approving energy infrastructure have failed twice before. The third time may be the charm, as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or BAAJA cleared its first procedural hurdle in the Senate on Monday. If it passes despite last-ditch opposition by environmental groups, it will massively boost America’s ability to scale up its electricity grid, on a three to-five year horizon. This will remove an important constraint on both AI data centers and manufacturing.

How Wuxi AppTec Stayed Sanction-Proof

2 Nov 2026

China’s two “Wuxi” biotech firms—AppTec and Biologics—are key partners for the US pharmaceutical industry, as contract developers and manufacturers of hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds. Washington lawmakers are increasingly uneasy about rising American reliance on the Wuxi firms. But their efforts to curb Wuxi’s access to the US market have been blocked, thanks to strong lobbying by the US pharma and biotech industries.

Power Lessons From China

26 Oct 2026

The US data center boom is facing a power crunch. So far, delays and cancellations due to electricity shortages have been sporadic but by some point in 2028, they could force a significant slowdown in data center construction. It will be important for the US to figure out how to better use batteries and distributed renewables generation to make power demand and supply more flexible. China is already ahead in this effort.

The State Of Chinese AI

19 Oct 2026

The AI world suffered tremors last week, as doubts began to surface about the frontier labs’ revenue growth and the rising amount of high-priced debt used to finance the US’s data center building binge. The risks raise a question: when and if the American AI bubble pops, can China race ahead? Probably not.

Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. While Chinese nuclear firms have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter.

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.
